newsitem.title: USA: Norfolk Southern debt deal moves full speed ahead.
newsitem.headline: Norfolk Southern debt deal moves full speed ahead.

text.p: Norfolk Southern Corp's highly sought after $4.3 billion mega-debt offering made a successful journey into the primary arena on Wednesday, carving itself a place in corporate bond history as well.

On Wednesday, the railroad firm sped ahead of U.S. West Inc's $4.1 billion debt offering to capture the title of largest investment-grade debt deal ever, according to research firm, Securities Data Co.
"Norfolk's deal was priced attractive...it'll trade at a spread premium in the secondary market," said one dealer.
"The attractiveness and oversubscription to it (deal) probably led to tighter spreads in surrounding issues," he added.
Buysiders confirmed the enthusiasm of dealers.

"To have a $4.3 billion deal right after CSX could have caused technical supply concerns," one money manager said. "And to see it work out this well gives you affirmation that there are sizeable buyers in this market."
Several weeks ago, CSX sold over $2 billion in bonds to finance its part of the acquisition.
In April, Norfolk Southern and CSX Corp, of Richmond, Va, agreed to a joint acquisition of Philadelphia-based Conrail for $10.3 billion.
Under the deal, Norfolk agreed to pay $5.9 billion for 58 percent of Conrail's assets. CSX agreed to pay $4.3 billion for remaining 42 percent of the east-coast railroad.
Another manager of a large fixed-income fund in New York said the depth of interest surpassed all expectations.
"The deal had everything big insurance companies were looking for and those managers bought the bulk of the issue," the manager said.
"It's a sector and name that people do not have a lot of, so insurance companies that have diversification needs were very aggressive purchasers," he added.
The bonds are also sure to be added to corporate-bond indexes, the managers said, making them a "must have" for those who tie performances to an index.

"This transaction is a vote of confidence in the reputation of Norfolk Southern as a good operator of a railroad company and for our financial strength," said William Romig, the company's vice president and treasurer.
He said the railroad company increased the offering to $4.3 billion from an original size of $3 billion as a result of strong investor demand for the bonds.
Analysts confirmed investors were optimistic about the outlook for the company.

"Basically, Norfolk Southern has been the best-run among the major railroads," said Gary Sparago, corporate bond analyst for Deutsch Morgan Grenfell. "They should be an even stronger competitor following integratation of the Conrail properties," he added.

Despite the positive market reception, one week prior to the offering, both Moody's and Standard & Poor's cut the credit rating of the company citing concerns about Norfolk's Southern increased debt load following the acquisition.
Romig said the company's goal is to restore its credit rating to the level prior to the merger through paying off the debt over time.
"It is our corporate objective to return to at least a single-A rating and improve our balance sheet going forward by paying down debt," Romig said. "We will turn our attention to doing that."

Norfolk Southern's offering consisted of eight different issues with maturities ranging from three years to 100 years. The BAA1/BBB-plus rated deal was jointly managed by Merrill Lynch & Co and JP Morgan Securities Inc.
In the broader corporate bond sector, investment-grade issues were seen tighter by a few basis points with better trading activity seen, high-grade traders said.
Players said the supermarket sector continued to perform well, paper was quoted better by about 1/4 point, high-yield traders said.
(( -- Nancy Leinfuss, 212-859-1675 ))
